blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The unit of observation is the thing each record describes: one child, one household, one village. A variable is a characteristic of that unit that can take different values across the units being studied. A characteristic that is the same for every unit is a constant, not a variable, and it carries no statistical information.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Think of a health worker’s register at a sub-centre. Each row is one person who walked in, the unit of observation. Each column (age, sex, vaccination status, haemoglobin) is a variable. One cell, one unit’s value on one variable, is one datum.

Not everything you could record is useful. If every person in your study lives in Chhattisgarh, “state of residence” distinguishes no one from anyone else. It is a constant. Age, sex and blood pressure differ from person to person, and that difference is exactly what statistics analyses. No variation, no statistics: this idea returns as the logic behind variance (roughly, the average squared distance of values from their mean, §3.6).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
At an under-five clinic you record, for every child: age in months, sex, nutritional status (normal / moderate wasting / severe wasting) and weight in kilograms. The unit is one child; the four characteristics are four variables. Before you can honestly say “the mean weight (the ordinary average, §2.2.1) of the children seen today was 11.8 kg”, you must have agreed, for every child, that weight was measured the same way, on the same scale, in the same units. Skip that agreement and the mean is meaningless however correctly you compute it.

Now suppose a study enrols only pregnant women attending an antenatal clinic. “Sex: female” is true for every unit, so within this dataset sex is a constant, even though it is a perfectly good variable in a general outpatient (OPD) register. Whether a characteristic is a variable depends on whether it varies within the units you are studying.

points.html: Variables are the columns of a dataset; units are the rows; one cell is one datum.
A characteristic identical across all units in your dataset is a constant and adds nothing to an analysis.
Analysis can rarely repair a variable that was badly defined or measured (“garbage in, garbage out”).

The type of a variable limits which summaries and tests are legitimate. Variables are classified two ways, by kind of value (§1.1.1) and by scale of measurement (§1.1.2). The two classifications overlap but are not identical.

blocks.html: Qualitative vs Quantitative Data

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A variable can vary in kind (a category) or in amount (a quantity). The first is qualitative (categorical) data. The second is quantitative (numerical) data, which splits into discrete data (separate, countable values, often whole numbers) and continuous data (any value within a range).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Sort a basket of fruit two ways. By type (apple, banana, mango) you group things by kind, and “apple” is neither more nor less than “banana”. By weight in grams, 150 g really is more than 100 g, and adding or averaging the numbers makes sense.

Ask of any variable: does it describe a category the unit falls into, or an amount the unit has? If a category, arithmetic is meaningless: averaging blood groups, (A + O) ÷ 2, produces nonsense even though a calculator will accept the codes. If an amount, arithmetic is legitimate.

Within amounts there is a second split. Some quantities move in separate steps: number of children, number of visits. You cannot have 2.5 children, so the variable is discrete. The steps need not be whole numbers (a score recorded in half-points is still discrete); what matters is that the possible values can be listed one by one. Others can fall anywhere on a scale: 62.3 kg is as valid as 62 kg. That is continuous.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the under-five register, nutritional status is qualitative (three categories). Weight in kilograms is quantitative and continuous: 11.2 kg sits meaningfully between 11 and 12. Number of diarrhoeal episodes in the past month is quantitative and discrete: 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 in this register, never 1.5. All three describe the same children; type is a property of each variable, not of the dataset.

points.html: Qualitative: attributes or categories; sums and means are not meaningful.
Quantitative: measurable amounts; arithmetic is meaningful. Discrete: separate, countable values (pregnancies, teeth). Continuous: any value within an interval (height, haemoglobin, blood pressure).
A continuous quantity is always recorded to finite precision (weight to 0.1 kg), but it stays continuous in nature. Classify by what the quantity is, not by how many decimals the scale shows.

This classification differs from the scales of measurement (§1.1.2), though qualitative data usually sit on nominal or ordinal scales and quantitative data on interval or ratio scales. Exams test both framings.
Misclassifying a variable leads straight to wrong analyses: a “mean” of a categorical variable, or a t-test (a test comparing two means, §9.2) run on category codes.

questions.prompt: Explain, without using the word “variable”, why “sex” might be a variable in one dataset but a constant in another.
questions.answer: In a general OPD register some records say “male” and others “female”, so sex tells you something that differs from one person to the next. In a dataset of pregnant women every record says “female”. There, sex is identical for every unit, so it carries no information that distinguishes one record from another: it is a constant in that dataset.

questions.prompt: A field worker records “type of latrine used” and later reports its “mean” across households. What is wrong with that statement, and what should be reported instead?
questions.answer: Type of latrine is qualitative (nominal): “pit latrine” and “flush toilet” are categories, not amounts, so averaging them (or their numeric codes) is meaningless. Report the frequency and percentage of households in each category, and the mode if one typical value is needed.

questions.prompt: The clinic register holds 100 children and 11 columns. How many data points (cells) does it contain? Classify “age in completed months” and “number of diarrhoeal episodes in the past month” as discrete or continuous, with a reason.
questions.answer: Cells = 100 × 11 = 1,100. Number of diarrhoeal episodes is discrete: it is a count (0, 1, 2 …) and 1.5 episodes is impossible. Age is continuous in nature (time passes continuously); “completed months” is a recording choice that rounds it down to whole months. As recorded, it takes only separate values (12, 13 … 36), so treating it as discrete is also acceptable if you state that it is age in completed months.

blocks.html: Scales of Measurement

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Scales of measurement classify a variable by which operations are meaningful on its values: equality, ordering, subtraction and division. There are four scales, each permitting everything the one below it permits plus one more operation: nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Think of a staircase of permissions:

  • Nominal: you may only check whether two values are the same or different.
  • Ordinal: you may also say one value is higher or lower than another.
  • Interval: you may also subtract, because the gaps between values are equal.
  • Ratio: you may also divide, because there is a true zero, so “twice as much” is a real statement.

Skip a step and you are doing invalid arithmetic. The classic slip is a ratio on an interval scale: 20°C is not “twice as hot” as 10°C, because 0°C is an arbitrary reference point, not “no heat”.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
• Blood group (A, B, AB, O): nominal. You can group, not order.
  • Pain severity (mild / moderate / severe): ordinal. Severe is worse than mild, but not by a fixed amount.
  • Temperature in Celsius: interval. The 10° gap between 10°C and 20°C equals the gap between 20°C and 30°C, but 0°C is not the absence of temperature.
  • Body weight in kg: ratio. 0 kg means no mass, so 20 kg really is twice 10 kg.

points.html: Nominal < ordinal < interval < ratio; each includes every operation of the ones before it.

The scale guides the choice of method, but it does not settle it alone. Nominal data are analysed with categorical-data methods: counts and percentages, the chi-square test (§10.6), exact tests (§10.7) and logistic regression (§13.2). Ordinal data suit rank-based methods (§10.1–10.5) or models for ordered categories (§13.2.7). Interval and ratio data permit means, standard deviations (SDs, a measure of spread, §3.7) and tests built on them, but whether such a test is appropriate also depends on its own assumptions, for example about the shape of the data’s distribution (§9.2.4, §10.1).

A single Likert item (strongly disagree … strongly agree) is ordinal. A summed Likert scale (the total of many items) takes many values and is routinely analysed with means and parametric methods (methods that assume a distribution shape, such as the normal; §9.2). Norman (2010) reviewed studies going back to the 1930s showing that such methods are robust for Likert data. Know the strict position for exams (median for an ordinal item) and the defensible practice for summed scales.
An interval scale has an arbitrary zero (ratios invalid); a ratio scale has a true zero (ratios valid). That single distinction separates the two.

blocks.html: Nominal Scale

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A nominal scale classifies values into named categories with no inherent order. The only meaningful operation is checking whether two units fall in the same category or different ones.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A nominal value is a label. Knowing someone’s blood group is A tells you nothing about “more” or “less” than group B; it tells you only that they differ from a person with B and match a person with A.

Numbers assigned for convenience in a database (Male = 1, Female = 2) are still labels. The “2” does not mean twice anything, and averaging the codes gives a number with no direct meaning as a measurement.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Blood group, religion, marital status, sex and diagnosis codes are nominal. In the community-based health insurance (CBHI) household survey, “reason for not joining” (lack of knowledge / lack of money / lack of trust / bad image / other) is nominal: five distinct categories with no ranking.

A nominal variable can be binary (dichotomous: two categories, e.g. CBHI member yes/no) or polychotomous (more than two, e.g. religion).

points.html: Only valid operation: equality or inequality. No ordering, no arithmetic.
The mode (the most frequent category, §2.4) is the only meaningful measure of central tendency.
Summarise with frequencies, proportions and percentages.

Association between two nominal variables is tested with the chi-square test of independence (§10.6.1); when expected cell counts are small (the rule is given in §10.6.1), Fisher’s exact test (§10.7) is used instead. The criterion is small expected counts, not a small sample as such.
Numeric codes carry no magnitude. The one exception worth knowing: for a binary variable coded 0/1, the mean of the codes equals the proportion coded 1.

blocks.html: Ordinal Scale

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: An ordinal scale classifies values into categories with a meaningful order, but the gaps between adjacent ranks are unequal or undefined.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Ordinal data add one capability to nominal data: you can say one value is higher or lower than another. You still cannot say by how much. Runners finishing 1st, 2nd and 3rd are ordered, but the ranks do not tell you whether 1st beat 2nd by a second or an hour, nor that the 1st–2nd gap equals the 2nd–3rd gap.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Cancer staging (Stage I–IV) is ordinal: Stage III is worse than Stage II, but the jump from I to II need not equal the jump from III to IV. Socioeconomic class on the modified Kuppuswamy scale (classes such as upper-middle, lower-middle, upper-lower and lower) is ordinal (Naaz et al., 2025). So is a single Likert-type response such as the CBHI survey’s 1-to-5 satisfaction item.

points.html: Valid operations: equality and ordering. Subtraction is not strictly valid, because gaps are not guaranteed equal.

The median (the middle value, §2.3) and the mode are the strictly appropriate measures of central tendency. Means of single ordinal items are common in applied work; know that this is a compromise (§1.1.2 on summed scales).

Rank-based methods (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis, Spearman correlation; §10.2–10.4, §11.3) use only the order of the values. Ordinal (cumulative-link) logistic regression (§13.2.7) models ordered categories directly and is often preferred once several predictors are involved.

blocks.html: Interval Scale

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: An interval scale has equal, meaningful gaps between values, so subtraction is valid, but its zero point is arbitrary, not a true absence of the quantity.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Interval data fix the unequal gaps of ordinal data: differences are now real quantities. The catch is zero. On an interval scale, zero is a reference point someone chose, so ratios stop making sense even though differences still do.

In Celsius, 0°C is the freezing point of water. So 20°C − 10°C = 10°C is meaningful, but “20°C is twice as hot as 10°C” is not. Convert to Fahrenheit (68°F vs 50°F) and the “ratio” changes, which shows it was never a property of the heat itself.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures are the textbook interval examples. The Kelvin scale measures the same quantity from absolute zero, so Kelvin is a ratio scale: 20°C and 10°C are 293.15 K and 283.15 K, a ratio of 1.035, nowhere near 2. The zero, not the quantity, makes the scale. IQ is another interval example: it is anchored at a population mean of 100, not at “zero intelligence”, so IQ 150 is not “1.5 times as intelligent” as IQ 100, though the 50-point difference is meaningful.

points.html: Valid operations: equality, order, subtraction. Division is not valid.
Means and SDs are legitimate, because differences are meaningful.
Interval-only variables are uncommon in clinical and community data. Almost every field measurement (weight, height, blood pressure, counts, durations) has a true zero and is therefore ratio-scaled.

blocks.html: Ratio Scale

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A ratio scale has equal, meaningful gaps and a true zero representing a genuine absence of the quantity, so division and ratio statements (“twice as much”) are meaningful.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Ratio data fix the one remaining problem of interval data. Because 0 kg truly means no mass, 20 kg really is twice 10 kg. Every operation from the lower scales (equality, order, subtraction) is available, plus division. There is no fifth level.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Body weight, height, blood pressure, haemoglobin, number of children, age and duration of illness are ratio-scaled: in each, zero means none of the quantity. A 20 kg child weighs twice as much as a 10 kg child, a statement that fails for Celsius temperature.

points.html: Valid operations: equality, order, subtraction, division.
Percentage-change statements become meaningful (“Group A’s mean weight is 20% higher than Group B’s”).

Being ratio-scaled permits means, SDs and methods such as the t-test (§9.2), ANOVA (§9.5), correlation (Chapter 11) and regression (Chapter 12); it does not guarantee they are appropriate. Each method has its own assumptions (independence, distribution shape, linearity, variance structure), listed where the method is taught (e.g. the assumptions of linear regression, §12.3).

questions.prompt: Without naming the four scales, describe the one extra “permission” each step up the measurement ladder unlocks.
questions.answer: First level: only same or different. Second: adds ordering (higher or lower). Third: adds meaningful subtraction, because gaps are equal. Fourth: adds meaningful division, because zero means none of the quantity.

questions.prompt: A colleague says “0°C means there is no heat.” Which scale is she confusing Celsius with? Convert 10°C and 20°C to kelvin and compute the true ratio of the two temperatures.
questions.answer:
She is treating Celsius (interval: arbitrary zero at the freezing point of water) as a ratio scale. Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so it is a ratio scale:

  1. 10°C = 10 + 273.15 = 283.15 K.
  2. 20°C = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K.
  3. Ratio = 293.15 ÷ 283.15 = 1.035.

20°C is about 3.5% “hotter” than 10°C in absolute terms, not twice as hot.

questions.prompt: In a dataset of 10 children, sex is coded Male = 1, Female = 2, and the “mean sex” comes out as 1.4. What, if anything, does 1.4 tell you?
questions.answer: As a measurement, nothing: the codes are labels. But because sex is binary, the mean of the codes has a hidden meaning. Mean = 1 + (proportion coded 2), so 1.4 = 1 + 0.4: 40% of the children (4 of 10) are girls. The correct report is “4 girls (40%) and 6 boys (60%)”; coding 0/1 would give 0.4 directly as the proportion.
